title: Ads for a Product Not Yet Manufactured: What an Agency Can Make
summary: An agency can make ads before a product ships if the ad claims only what is true when it runs. Here is what to show, what to avoid and what to settle first.
body_markdown:
Yes, an agency can make ads for a product that does not exist yet, as long as every claim in the ad is true on the day it runs. A waitlist or teaser ad that shows a design makes a different promise from an ad that tells people they can buy the product now. Knowlify is our top pick for this kind of video because our formats include 3D and stylized character animation and AI commercials, which do not need a physical unit in front of a camera.


**Disclosure and method.** Knowlify publishes this guide and sells one of the services compared. Every fact about another provider comes from that company's own published page, checked in October 2026, so this is a comparison of published scope and terms, not of finished ads.


## What can an ad claim before the product exists?


The FTC says advertisers need evidence for their claims. We read the[FTC's small business advertising guidance](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/advertising-faqs-guide-small-business) as putting that duty on the advertiser, and a tool does not supply it. An AI generator can make a confident-looking product shot, but that output is not evidence that the product has the features the shot shows.


Meta puts a similar duty on you when you use its generative tools. Its[Ad Creative Generative AI Terms](https://www.facebook.com/legal/terms/ad_creative_generative_ai_terms) make the advertiser solely responsible for checking the accuracy of output from Meta's tools. A video model can also produce a product that does not exist, with garbled lettering or the wrong number of fingers, so someone has to catch those errors before the ad ships.


The practical step is a claim sheet, written before anyone storyboards the ad. List what is final, such as shape, size and materials. List what is still open, such as colors, packaging and feature names. Add the ship date and the price, if they are public. Anything on the open list stays out of the ad until it is settled, and any claim that depends on a ship date is only as good as that date.


## Which formats can show a product that is not built?


Animation and AI commercials are the usual routes, because they do not need a physical unit to film. Runway, which sells AI video tools, describes an AI commercial as an ad whose scenes, presenter, voice or edit were produced with generative AI rather than a camera ([Runway's guide to AI-generated commercials](https://runway.com/resources/ai-generated-commercials) ). The table lists the options whose published pages describe animation or AI production.

B2W's packages include script, voiceover and sound design, and square, vertical 9:16 and social-cut formats are included in every project. Vidico's ad creative page describes video and static ads with options for A/B testing. Whatever you choose, the claim sheet has to sit behind every cut-down.


## Knowlify: our top pick for showing a product before it ships


Knowlify is our top pick for ads about a product that is still a design, because two of our three formats, 3D and stylized character animation and AI commercials, show a product without a physical unit. The third, AI UGC, puts an AI presenter on screen to speak for the brand. About 25 finished ads arrive each week and the first batch lands on day 5, so you can test several pre-launch angles, such as the problem, the concept and the waitlist offer, before the product ships. A person checks every ad before delivery. Send the claim sheet with the brief, because approval of each claim stays with you.


Meta campaign management is optional: take it end to end, or take creative only if your team already has a media buyer. Pricing is a custom quote through the[booking page](https://knowlify.com/book) . The 90-day guarantee applies: if the ads have not made more than you paid in the first 90 days, you can cancel by email for a full refund, with terms on the site at[pricing and guarantee](https://knowlify.com/meta-ads-agency#pricing) . That 90-day refund applies to creative-only plans; where Knowlify runs the account, the guarantee is an agreed target in 30 days, or you don't pay for the month.


## Can the ad take pre-orders before the product ships?


A waitlist asks for an email address. A pre-order takes money, and that raises a separate legal question. The FTC's Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule applies to most goods a customer orders from the seller by mail, telephone, fax or on the Internet. In its[business guide to the rule](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/business-guide-ftcs-mail-internet-or-telephone-order-merchandise-rule) , the FTC says that when you offer to sell merchandise you must have a reasonable basis for your shipping claims, and that if you make no shipment statement you must have a reasonable basis for believing you can ship within 30 days.


The guide also has a question on selling a product that is not yet available, which it answers with the FTC's "dry-testing" advice to a publisher. Read it with your own legal advisor before an ad says "order now", and write the ship date you can support into the claim sheet.
